summary: Laos admits fellow ASEAN nationals visa-free for up to 30 days (14 for a couple of members), plus Japan, South Korea, Russia, Switzerland and others on bilateral waivers. Nearly everyone else gets a 30-day tourist visa easily — online through the official Lao eVisa or on arrival at major airports and border crossings.

notes: Drug offences carry severe penalties in Laos, including the death penalty for trafficking.
Antiques and Buddha images require an export permit — buy religious artefacts only from licensed dealers.

payments.text: Cash is essential — cards work in upmarket hotels and some city restaurants, and ATMs in towns charge fees with low withdrawal caps. Thai baht and US dollars are widely accepted for larger purchases.

safety.text: Most visits are trouble-free; petty theft, motorbike bag-snatching and road accidents are the main risks. Unexploded ordnance remains a hazard well off marked paths in parts of the east, and banked river tubing in Vang Vieng has caused injuries.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Laos Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: November to February is the cool, dry season — ideal for Luang Prabang, Vientiane and the south. March to May is very hot and hazy from field burning, and June to October brings monsoon rain.

tips.text: Bring crisp US dollar notes — they pay for the visa on arrival, are accepted for many tourist services, and are a useful backup where ATMs are unreliable.

The Lao eVisa is accepted only at designated entry points — Vientiane and Luang Prabang airports and a handful of land crossings such as the first Friendship Bridge. Check the official list before planning an overland entry.
Unexploded ordnance from the 1960s-70s still contaminates parts of eastern and southern Laos — stay on marked paths and roads in rural areas and never touch metal objects found on the ground.
The kip has depreciated sharply in recent years, so prices for tours and hotels are often quoted in US dollars or Thai baht — carry a mix and check which currency a quote is in.
Cover shoulders and knees at temples, remove shoes before entering, and be discreet during the dawn alms round in Luang Prabang — keep your distance and never disrupt the monks.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Laos?
faq.answer: ASEAN nationals enter visa-free (30 days for most members, 14 for Myanmar and Brunei), and Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Russia and Mongolia have bilateral waivers. Almost everyone else — including US, UK, EU, Canadian and Australian passport holders — gets a 30-day tourist visa either online via laoevisa.gov.la or on arrival at major entry points.

faq.question: Should I get the Lao eVisa or a visa on arrival?
faq.answer: Both give a 30-day single-entry tourist stay. The eVisa (USD 50, about three business days online) skips the arrival queue but is accepted only at designated checkpoints; the visa on arrival (roughly USD 30-45 in cash, plus a photo) is available at all major airports and border crossings.

faq.question: Can I use the Lao eVisa at any border crossing?
faq.answer: No — it is honoured only at designated entry points, including Vientiane's Wattay and Luang Prabang international airports and the first Lao-Thai Friendship Bridge. Arriving anywhere else, get a visa on arrival or an embassy visa instead; check the current list on laoevisa.gov.la.

faq.question: Can I extend my stay in Laos?
faq.answer: Yes — 30-day tourist visas can be extended, typically by up to 30 additional days, at the immigration office in Vientiane or through local travel agents for a per-day fee. Overstays are fined per day on departure.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Laos?
faq.answer: Yes. US passport holders are not visa-exempt — apply online for the Lao eVisa (USD 50) before travel or obtain a 30-day tourist visa on arrival for a cash fee at major airports and border crossings.
